sentences: Snowflakes drift across a grey-blue sky, and five white egrets stand together in the falling snow.
This is Group of Egrets in Snow, a woodblock print designed by the Japanese artist Ohara Koson.
It was published in Tokyo by Watanabe Shōzaburō sometime between 1925 and 1936, and the image measures 36.2 centimetres high and 23.6 centimetres wide.
The Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam received it in 1999 as a gift from the collector Jan Perrée.
Look first at the birds.
White birds have been placed inside white snow, a quiet game of white upon white.
The artist set their pale feathers against the grey-blue ground, so that the same whiteness separates into falling snowflakes on one side and living birds on the other.
Now count the five birds one by one.
They stand in the same place, yet the bend of each neck and the way each one faces is slightly different.
Together they form a group, huddled close, but each one seems to be enduring the cold on its own terms.
Look at the snowflakes.
The print was made from a key block cut with black outlines, followed by several colour blocks printed one after another.
The swirling snow is a scatter of small white marks left on the paper.
Ohara Koson was born in Kanazawa in 1877 and died in Tokyo in 1945.
A master of kachō-e, prints of birds and flowers, he produced around five hundred designs during his career and worked under three names: Koson, Shōson and Hōson.
He was born Ohara Matao.
After training with the painter Suzuki Kason, he followed Japanese custom and took the name Koson, meaning son of Kason, in recognition of his debt to his teacher.

In his early years in Tokyo he made some triptychs showing episodes of the Russo-Japanese War, but birds and flowers were always the heart of his work, usually printed in flat colour in a tall, narrow, borderless format.
From around 1926 he worked with Watanabe and signed as Shōson.
Watanabe had coined the term shin-hanga, new prints, in 1915.
The movement kept the old ukiyo-e system, in which the designer, the carver, the printer and the publisher each did their own part, while bringing in the light and mood of Western painting.
Prints like this were sold mainly to the United States and Europe, because there was little interest in them at home.
Koson himself remained largely unknown in Japan for much of his career, and when his work became popular there from the 1970s onward, his prints had to be brought back from abroad.
Step back and look once more: white birds, white snow, and the silence between them.
Think of the people who would stand beside you on the coldest day of the year.
